title: Jerusalem was waiting for a king.
paragraphs: Jerusalem was waiting for a king.
Not just any king.
They were waiting for a conqueror.

For centuries, the Jewish people had lived under the shadow of foreign empires. Babylon had taken their city. Persia had ruled their land. Greece had spread its culture. And now Rome controlled their streets with soldiers and swords.
Every generation carried the same hope.
One day the Messiah will come.

A king like David.
A warrior like Joshua.
A ruler who would break the chains of oppression and restore Israel’s glory.
So when Jesus approached Jerusalem during Passover, the atmosphere was electric.
Thousands of pilgrims were already in the city.
Rumors had been spreading everywhere.

This was the man who healed the blind.
This was the man who multiplied bread.
This was the man who raised Lazarus from the dead.
People began to wonder:
Could this be the Messiah?
Then Jesus did something strange.
Instead of walking into the city like the other pilgrims, He asked for a donkey.
Not a horse.
A donkey.
At first glance, it seems like a small detail.
But in the ancient world, it meant everything.
Kings rode horses when they went to war.
They rode donkeys when they came in peace.
Jesus was making a statement before He even spoke a word.
As He entered the city, crowds began laying their cloaks on the road.
Palm branches filled the streets.
Voices rose in celebration:
“Hosanna to the Son of David!”
“Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!”
To them, this looked like the beginning of a revolution.
But Jesus knew something the crowd did not.
He was not entering Jerusalem to take a throne.
He was entering Jerusalem to carry a cross.
More than 500 years earlier, the prophet Zechariah had written these words:

“Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion!
Shout, Daughter Jerusalem!
See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey.”
— Zechariah 9:9
Jesus was intentionally fulfilling this prophecy.
He was revealing the true nature of His kingdom.
Not a kingdom built by violence.
A kingdom built by sacrifice.
Not a kingdom defended by swords.
A kingdom established by love.
Think about the contrast.
The people wanted a king who would destroy Rome.
Jesus came to destroy something far more dangerous.
Sin.
The crowd thought their greatest enemy was Caesar.
But humanity’s greatest enemy was sin, death, and separation from God.
And Jesus came to defeat all three.
Five days after the triumphal entry, the same city that shouted “Hosanna” would shout something very different.
“Crucify Him.”
The king they celebrated would be rejected.
The one who rode in on a donkey would walk out carrying a cross.
But this was never a tragedy outside of God’s plan.
This was the mission.
The donkey was not weakness.
It was a declaration.
Jesus was not the kind of king the world expected.
He was the kind of king the world desperately needed.
A king who conquers hearts instead of territories.
A king who forgives enemies instead of destroying them.
A king who would rather die for His people than demand they die for Him.
The triumphal entry reminds us of something deeply important.
Sometimes God answers our prayers in ways we don’t recognize.
The people prayed for deliverance.
God sent a Savior.
They wanted political freedom.
God offered eternal salvation.
They wanted a warrior.
God sent a Lamb.
And the Lamb would soon be sacrificed for the sins of the world.
But the story did not end at the cross.
Three days later, the King who rode into Jerusalem on a donkey would walk out of a tomb alive.
The peaceful king would prove He was also the victorious king.
Because the greatest victory in history was not won on a battlefield.
It was won on a cross.
And the empty tomb declared that the King who came in humility will one day return in glory.
The first time, He came riding on a donkey.
The next time, Scripture says He will come as the conquering King.
But on that day in Jerusalem, the message was clear:
God’s kingdom does not operate like the kingdoms of this world.
Power conquers enemies.
Love conquers hearts.
And the King who entered Jerusalem in humility became the Savior of the world.
So the next time you read about Jesus riding a donkey into Jerusalem, remember this:
It was not a random choice.
It was a message.
A message that the true King did not come to take life.
He came to give His.
And that is the kind of King worth following.
Engagement Question:
If you had been in the crowd that day, do you think you would have recognized the kind of King Jesus truly was? Why or why not?
